newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - June 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - June 25.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Wednesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Wachovia Corp has agreed to acquire Central Fidelity Banks for $2.3 billion in stock.
* The Dow Jones Industrials rebounded Tuesday, gaining 153.80 points to close at 7758.06, after plunging Monday over concerns about comments made by Japan Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

* Boeing may offer to change its sole-supplier agreements with three U.S. carriers in an attempt to pacify European Union regulators and overcome a major obstacle to its acquisition of McDonnell Douglas
* The index of consumer confidence reached its highest level in 28 years, according to the business research group Conference Board.
* Companies that make aids to stop smoking are fighting a marketing battle over a portion of the settlement with cigarette makers that calls for tobacco companies to provide up to $600 a smoker.
* The ABC television network has named Stu Bloomberg chairman of its entertainment division.
* Oracle Corp and Microsoft each have unveiled multimillion-dollar pledges to bring technology to schools and libraries.
* Royal Bank of Canada is i talks to acquire London Insurance Group.
* Edmund Jenkins, the former managing director of Arthur Andersen, has been named the new chairman of the Financial Accounting Standards Board.
* Saudi Arabia and Iran urged other cartel members to curtail crude production.
* The chairman of NASD is expected to propose reducing the size of its 47-member board to a 28-member parent board.
* Netscape and Microsoft have received U.S. government approval to export Internet software for banking that contains powerful security capabilities.
* Heard on the Street: Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette continues to be the topic of gossip among stock analysts who believe the firm is ripe for being bought out.
* Credit Markets: Apparent warnings from Prime Minster Ryutaro Hashimoto aside, Japan is unlikely to sell its holds of U.S. Treasury securities any time soon.
